authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Return to sender: Milotic makes Sunyshore pay
articles.dek: Traded to Violet in Week 5, Milotic scored on an interception and forced the fumble that set up another touchdown in the Falcons’ 33–20 win.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore sent Milotic to Violet. Milotic sent the football back 52 yards for a touchdown. Of all the ways the Starseekers could have lost their unbeaten record, arranging delivery of the opposing defensive player of the game is going to be the hardest one to explain.

The cornerback was part of a six-player package Sunyshore traded to the Falcons in Week 5. Before that week was over, No. 89 had intercepted Jolt Vick, forced and recovered Nair Jordan's fumble, and helped turn those mistakes into 14 Violet points. The Falcons won 33–20. You don't need a particularly elaborate calculator to see why his old club might prefer to discuss something else.
I picked Sunyshore. I liked its defense, and I thought it could carry a week without DeZhaun Watzon. Milotic has supplied a fairly pointed review of that argument.
The forwarding address worked.
body.speaker: Milotic

body.text: The first delivery came with 2:54 left in the opening quarter. Violet already led 6–0, and Sunyshore had produced one yard on the first two plays of its second drive. On third-and-nine, Vick threw deep left. Milotic intercepted it and returned it for a touchdown. A conversion later, the Starseekers were down 13 before their offense had made a first down.

It was a dreadful setting for an emergency starter: long yardage, a growing deficit and a cornerback who suddenly had a very personal place in the afternoon. Vick's interception mattered enormously. So did the two runs that left him trying to solve third-and-nine. Sunyshore's opening three drives produced four yards and ended with two punts and Milotic's score.

Violet didn't need a touchdown drive to build a 16–0 lead. Loudred made field goals from 53, 49 and 24 yards, while Zebstrika returned the first two Sunyshore punts 20 and 41 yards. Sunyshore was conceding ground between its defensive series, then asking the defense to defend what was left.
Fourteen points with a familiar name

The Starseekers finally put together a 73-yard touchdown drive, with Scol Alexander finishing from three yards. Fred Whirler then sacked Iron Jugulis on third-and-one. At 16–7, Sunyshore had a stop and a chance to make the game much less strange before halftime.
Milotic interrupted.

At 1:09, Vick completed a short-right pass to Nair Jordan for no gain. Jordan fumbled; Milotic recovered. Two seconds later on the game clock, Iron Jugulis threw short right to Carnivine for a touchdown. Violet's scoring drive was one play. Sunyshore's traded cornerback had supplied the invitation.

The final accounting credited Milotic with three tackles, an interception, a pass defended, a forced fumble, a recovery and a touchdown. Those aren't decorative additions to a winning box score. The two takeaways created the game's most expensive swings, and they belonged to a player the losing team had just chosen to move.
We made the trade. We also threw that pass and lost that ball. I'm not going to stand here and turn Milotic's day into an accident. He made the plays.
body.speaker: Karson Jones

body.text: Vick kept playing. His seven-play response covered 75 yards in 44 seconds and ended with an 18-yard touchdown pass to Fera LaGatr. A missed extra point left it 23–13 at halftime. Later, Vick found MF STOMP for a 21-yard touchdown on third-and-nine, cutting Violet's lead to 26–20 with 50 seconds left in the third quarter.

There was enough offense to win this game. Vick completed 20 of 31 passes for 201 yards and two touchdowns without taking a sack. Sunyshore finished ahead in total yards and first downs, and converted six of twelve third downs. Its line kept the quarterback upright. Its quarterback recovered from the early interception. The rest of the afternoon kept creating new bills.
Third-and-nine, deep left. That's the interception. I don't want it described as something that happened to us. I threw it. But we got back to six points down, and I still thought we could finish it.
body.speaker: Jolt Vick

body.text: The stop that never came
Violet's next drive is why this can't become only a trade story. With the lead down to six, Iron Jugulis took the Falcons 75 yards for the touchdown that restored a two-score margin.

Zack Bear's sack had set up third-and-ten at the start of the fourth quarter. Zangoose ran up the middle for eleven yards. A defense that had just created the down it wanted couldn't finish it. Two plays later, Iron Jugulis found Furret deep right for 26 yards; the quarterback eventually scored from one yard at 4:38.

Furret caught seven passes for 147 yards, including gains of 44, 28, 26 and 24. That was a repeated route to large chunks of the field, not one broken play hidden inside an otherwise quiet day. Zebstrika added a 69-yard punt return in the third quarter, completing a three-return, 130-yard assault on Sunyshore's punt coverage.
An upset? We were open. Call it that.
body.speaker: Furret

body.text: Sunyshore's last drive included Vick's 42-yard completion to Jordan, but ended on an incomplete fourth-and-three pass to Buizel with 4:02 remaining. Violet kept the ball for the rest of the game.

The Starseekers are 4–1. The Falcons are 2–3. Those records will keep Sunyshore above Violet in plenty of arguments about the season, including mine. This particular argument belongs to No. 89: one interception, one forced fumble, one recovery, and a forwarding address Sunyshore won't forget.

articles.title: Flock takes the express route
articles.dek: Marshall Flock’s 95- and 93-yard kickoff-return touchdowns turn Mossdeep’s 49–3 victory into a special-teams showcase.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Marshall Flock made Fuchsia pay for scoring. Then he made Fuchsia pay for halftime. Two kickoffs, two touchdowns, 188 yards, and a very clear lesson for anyone preparing to send the ball toward Mossdeep's No. 44: the field is shorter for him than it looks from your end.

The Eclipse won 49–3 and moved to 5–0. Flock, the Swellow listed at halfback, carried only four times. He was still the player of the game. His eight returns produced 314 yards and the two touchdowns that pulled the game away from Fuchsia before Dram Marino needed to spend much of the second half finishing it.

A week after Mossdeep needed a late interception and a last-minute drive to survive at Dewford, this was a welcome change in working conditions. The offense scored five touchdowns. The defense allowed none. Flock supplied two more without asking either unit for another snap.
I like giving the offense a short walk back to the bench.
body.speaker: Marshall Flock

body.text: The first return was especially rude. Fuchsia had just spent fourteen plays moving 46 yards for Clamperl's 40-yard field goal. There were fourth-down yards to earn and repeated tackles to survive. That kick cut Mossdeep's lead to 7–3 with 27 seconds left in the first quarter. The Shadows had finally put something on the scoreboard.

Flock returned the ensuing kickoff 95 yards for a touchdown. Adam Vinathorn's extra point made it 14–3 with eleven seconds left. Fuchsia had used nearly half a quarter to get three points; Mossdeep had answered with seven before the quarter ended. That exchange belongs near the top of any explanation of this game.

The second return came on the opening kickoff of the third quarter. Flock went 93 yards for another touchdown. Mossdeep had led 21–3 at halftime; now it was 28–3 before its offense had run a second-half play. There was no gradual squeeze left to describe. Fuchsia was chasing a game that kept accelerating away from it.
Marshall changed the score twice without Dram touching the ball. He deserves his name at the top of this one. The rest of us can take a turn below it.
body.speaker: Michael Dorrill

body.text: Diggs has his own day

Marino's receivers were hardly spectators. Driflon Diggs caught seven passes for 73 yards and two touchdowns, giving Mossdeep another important story inside a result that will usually be remembered for Flock.

Diggs' first touchdown came on a deep-left throw for 21 yards with 55 seconds left in the second quarter. He had already started that four-play scoring drive with a seven-yard catch to the right. Ninjulio Jones caught a 13-yard pass and ran for four before Marino returned to Diggs. Four plays, three different touches by receivers, and a touchdown before halftime.

The second Diggs score came from six yards with 3:24 left in the fourth. By then the outcome was settled. The contribution still matters for an offense whose injury report now lists Accel BeckhmJr out one week. BeckhmJr caught two passes for 26 yards in this game; Diggs gave the Eclipse substantial receiving production on an afternoon when their usual options were changing.
Accel's been doing this longer than I have. I don't like seeing his name on that report. I'm happy about the touchdowns. I'd rather have him asking for the next target, too.
body.speaker: Driflon Diggs

body.text: Gronkaludon added five catches for 87 yards. His third-quarter touchdown drive was almost comically brief: Marino threw deep left to him for twenty yards, then short right for thirty-one and the score. That is a tight end taking an entire drive for himself, with a quick change of direction between receptions.

Marino finished 18-of-23 for 225 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Mossdeep needed only four third-down attempts. Fuchsia faced fourteen. I prefer that comparison to a long speech about offensive rhythm: one team repeatedly kept the chains out of the conversation; the other repeatedly had to negotiate with them.

The ground game helped. Ninjaskamara's ten carries gained 94 yards, including the two-yard touchdown that opened Mossdeep's scoring. Jones scored on a seven-yard run early in the fourth. The Eclipse gained 128 yards on seventeen rushing attempts, making the short passing game an option instead of an obligation.
Fuchsia couldn't find a second score

Empoleon attempted 34 passes, completed fifteen and threw an interception to Electric Berry. The Shadows also lost a fumble, and Mossdeep collected four sacks. Clay Rathews supplied two of them. Fuchsia's longest scoring contribution was still the field goal that Flock had answered almost immediately.

Berry's interception came in the second quarter, and his final line included four tackles and a fumble recovery. The defensive player of the game accepted a much quieter kind of attention than the returner.
Marshall's the interview. I just wanted the ball back.
body.speaker: Electric Berry

body.text: There are reasons this victory felt easier than the one at Dewford, and the opponent is among them: Fuchsia fell to 0–5. But ease still has to be produced. Mossdeep did it through clean passing, productive runs, takeaways and a returner who turned two routine restarts into touchdowns. That is a fuller explanation than pointing at the teams' records and closing the notebook.

The Eclipse have scored 203 points in five games. Forty-nine came here. Fourteen of those arrived with Flock carrying a kickoff through the entire scoring argument, and the two distances look almost mischievous beside each other: 95, then 93.

articles.title: The Reds survive. The next six weeks just got harder.
articles.dek: Josh Alakazam throws three touchdowns and Foo Warner seals a 24–20 win, but Garshawn Lynch’s six-week absence changes Mt. Silver’s season.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Mt. Silver left Oreburgh unbeaten and considerably less comfortable. The 24–20 victory preserved the Reds' perfect start. The six-week injury listing beside Garshawn Lynch's name changed the part of the season that comes next. One of those facts fits neatly in the standings. The other is going to occupy Connor McLarren for a while.

Lynch caught an eighteen-yard touchdown pass late in the second quarter and gained 44 yards on seven carries. His season rushing total stands at 672. Now the league's leading rusher is out for six weeks, and the Reds must find out how much of their offense travels without him.

It would be a peculiar afternoon to call easy. Oreburgh, now 1–4, led twice in the first half, cut the deficit to one point in the fourth quarter and had the ball twice with a chance to take the lead or win. Mt. Silver needed a fourth-down breakup by Tauros Woodson and a late interception by Foo Warner to finish it.

Vibrava got forty-six on the ground! Write that down. I'm annoyed about missing time, obviously, but don't interview me like the rest of them have vanished. Josh can still throw it. You've seen Josh throw it.
body.speaker: Garshawn Lynch

body.text: Josh Alakazam could, and did. He completed nineteen of twenty-four passes for 230 yards and three touchdowns. Ariados, Lynch and Scep Smith Jr. caught the scoring passes. The Reds' three touchdown drives covered 67, 73 and 73 yards, which is a convincing demonstration of an offense capable of building its own opportunities.

It also explains why this game stayed in their hands after a difficult beginning. Alakazam's first drive ended with Medicham intercepting a deep-right pass on second-and-one. Oreburgh used the next drive to score, with Cryogonal finding Marshtomp from three yards at the start of the second quarter. Mt. Silver had put yards together and received nothing; Oreburgh had turned its chance into the lead.

Alakazam responded with the touchdown pass to Ariados. When Cryogonal found Furret for a fourteen-yard score, Alakazam responded again, this time with the short-right throw Lynch carried for eighteen yards and a touchdown. The game reached halftime tied at fourteen. For all the Reds' reputation, Oreburgh hadn't spent the half behaving like a supporting character.
I prefer the drives that end with someone else holding the ball. The interception was a poor attempt at that.
body.speaker: Josh Alakazam

body.text: Oreburgh keeps the door open

Mt. Silver's first drive of the second half ended with Alakazam finding Scep Smith Jr. for a nine-yard touchdown. That put the Reds ahead 21–14. Then the Miners began using time and smaller gains to work their way back.

A twelve-play drive ended with Marshtomp's 44-yard field goal. On the next Mt. Silver series, Plusico Buress fumbled after an eleven-yard reception and Stunfisk recovered. Oreburgh drove for another field goal, this one from 39 yards. With 2:39 remaining, the Reds led 21–20.

There is an uncomfortable number in the middle of that comeback: Oreburgh converted eight of thirteen third downs. The Reds converted four of six themselves, but their defense kept having to stay on the field. This was the opposite of the previous week's 36–6 win over Lavender, when Mt. Silver had seemed capable of deciding when every part of the game would happen.

The Miners weren't producing the larger offensive total. They finished with 218 yards against Mt. Silver's 319. They were keeping the contest close enough that the next mistake could matter. Buress' fumble mattered. So did the stop Oreburgh made after its second field goal, forcing the Reds to punt with a one-point lead.
The record says five wins. It doesn't say we can afford to give the ball away twice. We had to defend the result after that, and Tauros and Foo made two plays we needed very badly.
body.speaker: Connor McLarren

body.text: At 1:27, Cryogonal threw deep left on fourth-and-four. Tauros Woodson broke up the pass. Mt. Silver took over and gave Vibrava three consecutive runs: five yards left, four up the middle, one right. The first down let the Reds work the clock before Venusaur's 33-yard field goal made it 24–20 with 39 seconds left.

That field goal changed the final task. Oreburgh needed a touchdown. Cryogonal found Furret for seven yards, spiked the ball, then threw short right. Foo Warner intercepted with 24 seconds on the clock and returned it seventeen yards. Alakazam knelt once. Only then could the game be described in the past tense.
A different unbeaten team

Vibrava's nine carries for 46 yards deserve attention beyond Lynch's enthusiastic recommendation. They are actual production from another runner in a game the Reds had to win. That doesn't automatically make Vibrava the answer to six weeks without the league leader, but it gives the discussion a player and a set of carries instead of a vague promise about depth.

Alakazam also spread his nineteen completions across the offense. Gregar Jenings gained 68 receiving yards, Scep Smith Jr. 67, and Tony Gyarzalez added three catches. Mt. Silver has people to involve. The harder question is how the attack changes when opponents can prepare without Lynch at its center.

Oreburgh deserves credit for making this conversation happen under pressure. A one-win team had the ball late against an unbeaten one and forced the favorite to execute. The Miners' last chance ended in Warner's hands; it was a chance all the same.
The Reds are 5–0. Lynch has 672 rushing yards. For the next six weeks, that second number won't move.

articles.title: Saffron scores 48. Lavaridge may keep the zero.
articles.dek: HeeDee Lamb piles up 266 yards from scrimmage, Verrick Brooks records four sacks, and the Psi Corps deliver their third shutout.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Saffron has developed an inconsiderate habit of making its opponents' offensive statistics optional reading. Lavaridge lost 48–0, the Psi Corps recorded their third shutout, and HeeDee Lamb produced enough offense to require a second line on the receipt. I suspect the Inferno would prefer the version with just the final score. It leaves out quite a lot.

Lamb caught ten passes for 204 yards and ran ten times for another 62. He scored once each way. Verrick Brooks collected four sacks. Archiekazam threw four touchdown passes without taking a sack himself. The traveling Psi Corps won the argument early, then spent the rest of the game submitting additional documentation.

This was Saffron's fourth straight victory after the 10–9 opening loss to Vermilion. Yes, I remember that result. No, this is not an invitation to discuss it. The Psi Corps have allowed twenty points across five games, and Lavaridge didn't contribute any of them.
Ten carries, ten catches. That's a pleasant way to divide an afternoon. I don't need every touch to look the same.
body.speaker: HeeDee Lamb

body.text: Lamb's four-yard run to the right opened the scoring with 3:24 left in the first quarter. Saffron had needed five plays to cover 44 yards. The Inferno had already punted once; they would do so seven times before the game ended. Their offense produced three successful third downs in sixteen attempts, which is a long afternoon of walking back toward the sideline.

Saffron didn't need its offense for the second touchdown. Jolteon returned a punt 88 yards early in the second quarter, turning Grubbin's 49-yard kick into seven more points for the visitors. At 14–0, the Psi Corps had touchdowns from a receiver's run and a returner's work. Archiekazam hadn't yet thrown his first scoring pass.

He found Venomoth deep right for fifteen yards at 2:16, giving Saffron its third touchdown before halftime. That throw completed a five-play, 65-yard drive. The efficiency was almost impolite: the Psi Corps were going a long way without giving Lavaridge many opportunities to interrupt.
HeeDee makes the next throw easier. They have to account for him, and Venomoth still has a route. I don't mind sharing the explanation.
body.speaker: Archiekazam

body.text: The zero took work

Lavaridge's best first-half drive lasted seventeen plays and gained 62 yards. It ended on downs. The Inferno had managed to keep the ball, move it and make Saffron defend an extended series. They still went to halftime down 21–0.

That is the part of a shutout that disappears when the score becomes enormous. A defense has to protect it before the margin is comfortable, when a touchdown could still change the game. Saffron did that. The long Lavaridge drive produced more opportunities for a mistake and never got the one it needed.

Brooks made the rest especially difficult. All four sacks of Delphox belonged to the Victreebel wearing No. 52. His season total reached eleven. There are plenty of teams that would enjoy having one player produce that kind of problem; Lavaridge had the less enjoyable task of blocking him.
Four sacks. I like a number that fits on a leaf.
body.speaker: Verrick Brooks

body.text: The defense's success also freed the offense from urgency. Gorebyss made field goals from 48 and 40 yards in the third quarter. Those six points increased the lead to 27–0, and there was no requirement to make every drive spectacular. Saffron could take the points while Lavaridge kept searching for its first ones.

Then the fourth quarter supplied the spectacular again. Archiekazam found Pawmo from a yard out on third-and-one. Lamb caught a thirteen-yard touchdown to the left. Venomoth added an eleven-yard scoring catch with nineteen seconds left. Three touchdown passes in the quarter turned a decisive victory into a number that will be read aloud on every preview show.

The final touchdown followed Pachirisu's interception and 47-yard return. Even after Archiekazam had thrown a late interception of his own, Saffron's defense gave the offense another short assignment. The Psi Corps finished with 383 yards, but they didn't insist on gaining all of them at once.
I had forty-one attempts. I can't tell you there wasn't a chance to do more with them. I can tell you I don't want anyone explaining my afternoon for me.
body.speaker: Delphox

body.text: A team with more than one headline

The temptation is to place Lamb's 266 scrimmage yards above everything else. I won't argue strenuously. Ten catches for 204 yards would have carried a feature by itself; adding ten runs creates a much more troublesome player for a defense to organize around.

But Venomoth caught five passes for 78 yards and two touchdowns. The return unit scored. The kicker made both field-goal attempts and all six extra points. The quarterback had room to throw. Saffron's superiority arrived from too many directions for Lavaridge to fix it with one better matchup.

The Inferno fell to 2–3 after a second straight loss. Delphox finished with 169 passing yards on 41 attempts, and Lavaridge's nineteen runs gained 43 yards. The offense spent too much of the game needing another conversion, another manageable down, another way past Brooks. It found too few of each.

Saffron is 4–1, with a defense that has allowed four points per game. I expect someone will eventually explain why that average is misleading. Until then, Lavaridge's contribution is available for inspection: zero.

art.alt: HeeDee Lamb, Heliolisk No. 11, running in Saffron pink and blue.

articles.title: Four kicks beat the whole Stone offense
articles.dek: Unown goes four-for-four, Disa-Disa-Disa misses the late go-ahead attempt, and Pewter escapes Rustboro with a 12–10 win.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Rustboro found 163 rushing yards, a touchdown and several ways to make its own afternoon miserable. Pewter found Unown. The kicker went four-for-four, including two makes from 52 yards, and the Rockers won 12–10 without scoring a touchdown. If you're looking for a grand strategic explanation, start with the foot.

I'm inclined to like a Stone game built around Philly. Nineteen carries for 97 yards and a touchdown is a perfectly respectable reason. I'm less inclined to admire what Rustboro did with the chances surrounding those carries. Two lost fumbles and a missed late field goal turned a game the Stone could have won into one they'll have to explain.

Pewter's last points came on Unown's 27-yard kick with 5:22 left. Rustboro had time for two substantial drives after that. The first ended with a fumble. The second ended with Disa-Disa-Disa's 40-yard field goal going wide left with 43 seconds remaining. The margin was two. The missed opportunity was larger.
Four. It's a good shape.
body.speaker: Unown

body.text: Unown's first two kicks were the impressive ones: 52 yards in the opening quarter and another 52 in the second. Rustboro had answered the first with a fourteen-play, 82-yard touchdown drive, Philly carrying up the middle from a yard out. The Stone had built the kind of series that makes a running back look like a sensible investment.

Then the offense began spending its success. A nine-play drive gained 34 yards and ended in a punt. Late in the half, Philly lost a fumble on a third-and-ten run, and Swampert recovered for Pewter. The Rockers turned that opening into Unown's 29-yard field goal with four seconds left. Rustboro went to halftime trailing 9–7 despite having scored the game's only touchdown.
Ninety-seven yards doesn't cancel the fumble. I know. You can put both numbers in. Just don't act like I spent the other eighteen carries hiding.
body.speaker: Philly

body.text: It's a fair demand. Philly repeatedly gave Rustboro something to build around. Watchog added 53 yards on five carries, and the team gained more than five yards per rushing attempt overall. The ground game supplied a real advantage. It wasn't enough to rescue every failed throw or every loose ball.

Frosmoth completed ten of twenty-six passes for 93 yards. Pewter recorded eight passes swatted, and Rustboro never threw a touchdown. The quarterback wasn't sacked. That makes protection a particularly unconvincing place to hide the passing performance. The Rockers were disrupting throws without needing to put him on the ground.
The gift, then the repayment

Rustboro received a major chance early in the third quarter when Froslass fumbled a punt return and Solrock recovered. The Stone used the next drive for Disa-Disa-Disa's 32-yard field goal, taking a 10–9 lead at 3:02.

That was an opportunity converted into points, but only three. The distinction became painful when Pewter assembled its fifty-yard field-goal drive across the end of the third quarter and the start of the fourth. Unown's fourth make restored the lead. The Rockers had scored three points four times; Rustboro had no answer that counted afterward.

The Stone's next drive consumed twelve plays and gained 42 yards. On third-and-ten at 2:28, Frosmoth completed a thirteen-yard pass to Glimmet. It should have been the conversion Rustboro needed. Glimmet fumbled, and Tranquill recovered for Pewter. A play that moved the chains instead moved the ball to the other team.
Ten completions in twenty-six attempts. That's my number. We had a conversion on the Glimmet play, then we lost the ball. Before that, there were too many throws that gave us nothing.
body.speaker: Frosmoth

body.text: The defense kept the Stone alive again. Pewter punted, leaving Rustboro 1:49 to find a field goal. Frosmoth completed an eight-yard pass to Huntail on third-and-three. Philly ran for seven. There was a route to a very different ending, and Rustboro had already taken several steps along it.

Then an incomplete pass intended for Diggersby, broken up by Mightyena, left another third-and-three. Nuzleaf ran up the middle and lost a yard to Swampert. Disa-Disa-Disa came on for the 40-yard attempt at 0:43. Wide left. Delcatty's eight-yard run on the next snap used the rest of the game.
Our defense kept giving us a chance to finish it. We had the ball after the last field goal, we had it after the fumble, and we had the kick. I can't ask for a fourth ending.
body.speaker: Tyler Scarboro

body.text: Pewter's offense produced 194 yards and only two third-down conversions. It didn't suddenly become explosive. The Rockers did make every field-goal attempt, recover two fumbles and prevent Rustboro from turning its yardage advantage into a second touchdown. At 3–2, they'll accept that combination without requiring it to look handsome.

Rustboro dropped to 2–3. Armaldo's thirteen tackles and the productive rushing day will survive as good individual work in a losing box score. The decisive comparison is much shorter than that box score: Unown, four-for-four. Disa-Disa-Disa, one-for-two. The last attempt went left.

art.alt: Philly, Gabite No. 63, in Rustboro brown and silver beside a football.

articles.title: Lavender finds two points worth keeping
articles.dek: A 52-yard field goal and two late defensive recoveries help the Wails hold off Hearthome 17–15 and reach their bye at 4–1.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender needed a win it could hold, not a performance it could frame. After the thirty-point defeat at Mt. Silver, the Wails went to Hearthome, made just enough plays, and left with a 17–15 victory. It was untidy and occasionally alarming. It also sent them into their bye at 4–1, which is a rather good place to spend a week considering the untidiness.

The final difference came from two points Hearthome never scored. After Frosmoth's four-yard touchdown pass to Wiglett cut the lead to 17–15, the Haunts tried to tie the game. Vibrava ran up the middle, lost a yard and fumbled; Arcanine recovered for Lavender. The two-point attempt failed with 2:17 left.

Hearthome still got the ball back. Lavender still had to defend the lead. At 1:34, Vibrava fumbled again on a run up the middle, and this time Muk recovered. Diggersby supplied the first down the Wails needed, and Mr. Clanky finished with two kneels. The last two minutes had offered plenty of reasons to worry. Lavender kept the two-point margin through all of them.
The kneels were my favorites.
body.speaker: Mr. Clanky

body.text: That is a reasonable review from a quarterback who had spent much of the afternoon working harder for less. Clanky completed seventeen of twenty-nine passes for 163 yards, threw a touchdown and avoided interceptions. The Wails converted only two of eleven third downs. Their offense repeatedly had to find another way to keep a drive alive or hand the problem back to the defense.

The touchdown pass arrived on fourth-and-four. Trailing 6–0 in the second quarter, Clanky found Beedrill short left for six yards and a score with 1:33 remaining. Lavender had taken twelve plays to travel 68 yards. This was no leisurely response to the early deficit; it required the quarterback to make the conversion on the final available down.

Hearthome had opened the scoring on a fifteen-yard deep-right pass from Frosmoth to Castform at 5:42 of the second quarter. Sunflora missed the extra point. That missed point didn't seem likely to dominate the game at the time. By the fourth quarter, every piece of the arithmetic had acquired a much sharper edge.
We were going to get asked about Mt. Silver whatever happened here. I'd rather get asked at four-and-one. The fourth-down throw to Beedrill gave us a chance to make that the conversation.
body.speaker: Travis Scarboro

body.text: The best minute of the afternoon

After Beedrill's touchdown, the Wails forced a quick punt. Their next drive started with 1:11 left in the half. Seven plays and 58 yards later, Kricketune ran up the middle from one yard for the touchdown that made it 14–6 after the extra point.

Those two late first-half scores carried much of Lavender's day. The Wails had spent the opening quarter without a point and had already punted twice before their first touchdown. Then they put together consecutive scoring drives before halftime. It was the most convincing stretch of offensive football they produced, and it gave the defense something worth protecting.

Diggersby finished with 64 yards on thirteen carries. Carnivine caught five passes for 53 yards; Frosmoth added two catches for 43. Beedrill's six receptions gained only 38 yards, but one ended in the end zone on fourth down. The numbers tell different stories depending on which one you read first. Lavender will happily begin with that touchdown.

Hearthome opened the second half with a twelve-play drive and Sunflora's 39-yard field goal. The Haunts had narrowed the lead to 14–9 and given the Wails a familiar sort of afternoon: every stalled drive threatened to make the next defensive series feel enormous.

Lavender's kicker, Just a cactus, changed the margin with a 52-yard field goal at 5:36 of the fourth quarter. It was his only field-goal attempt. The kick pushed the lead to eight, requiring Hearthome to find a touchdown and a conversion to draw level. The Haunts eventually found the first. The second stayed out of reach.
I'm glad they trusted the distance. Fifty-two is a long way to spend watching the ball, even when you're the one who kicked it.
body.speaker: Just a cactus

body.text: Hearthome's touchdown came after a short, four-play scoring drive. On third-and-four, Frosmoth found Wiglett short left for four yards. There was no spare margin in the conversion itself: four needed, four gained, six points. That brought the Haunts to fifteen and sent Vibrava into the failed two-point attempt.
One more stop was required

Lavender then punted again. This is why the failed conversion can't stand alone as the ending. Hearthome took over with 1:44 left and still had time to win with a field goal. The Wails had to get the ball back, and Muk's recovery did it.

Hearthome's Frosmoth finished with two touchdown passes and no interceptions. Swampert made fourteen tackles. There were performances worth keeping for the Haunts, who fell to 1–4, but the late fumble denied them the chance to turn those performances into a different record.
Don't tell me we were nearly good enough. We had the ball with time to win. That's the part I'm going to remember.
body.speaker: Frosmoth

body.text: Lavender outgained Hearthome 259–206 and avoided a turnover. The Wails also punted five times, struggled on third down and needed a late recovery to protect the result. I don't think anyone who watched should confuse this with a comfortable win. I do think a team recovering from its first defeat is allowed to value the win without first making it beautiful.
The bye arrives with four victories, one loss and a little room to breathe. Clanky's final two plays gained minus-two yards. They were, as he said, his favorites.

art.alt: Mr. Clanky, Iron Bundle No. 11, in Lavender violet and black.

articles.title: Yes, I enjoyed the other 46 points, too
articles.dek: Mara Voss on a 49–3 win, a returner who kept skipping the commute, and the perfectly reasonable pleasure of watching Mossdeep stay unbeaten.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I spent last week worrying about what Mossdeep would lose without Tyran Armstead. Then the Eclipse won 49–3. You may imagine that this has made me reluctant to revisit my concerns. On the contrary, I have prepared a very balanced response: forty-nine points, three allowed, please leave the arithmetic on the screen.

Marshall Flock returned two kickoffs for touchdowns. Marino threw three more. Ninjaskamara and Ninjulio supplied the rushing scores. There were enough ways into the end zone that the defense could have requested a quieter afternoon and still received one. I enjoyed it. I don't intend to disguise that enjoyment as an advanced statistical conclusion.

Last week's column asked what survives a missing piece. The answer against Fuchsia was quite a lot. The protection allowed one sack, Marino completed eighteen of twenty-three passes, and Mossdeep never needed to turn the game into a referendum on one absent tackle. Armstead is now clear of the injury report. The test was useful. Getting him back is useful, too.

I also remember Dewford. A week earlier, Mossdeep needed a late field goal to win 23–20. The Breakers subsequently beat Cinnabar. Anyone trying to sell the Eclipse's narrow escape as proof of an ordinary team has acquired an inconvenient additional result. Dewford looked capable against Mossdeep and kept looking capable afterward. That is how a close win can improve with age.
Permission to enjoy a good thing

Five-and-zero is a lovely record. A scoring margin of plus-163 makes it lovelier. The Eclipse have scored 203 points and allowed forty. These are actual things that happened, and I would like to spend a paragraph enjoying them before somebody asks how well a kickoff return predicts the next kickoff return.

It doesn't have to predict anything to have won this game. Flock's 95-yard return answered Fuchsia's field goal with twenty-four seconds left in the first quarter. His 93-yard return opened the second half. Between them, the visitors experienced the peculiar discomfort of kicking off twice and immediately defending an extra point twice. I imagine the next kickoff felt longer than usual.

Flock was credited with 314 return yards on eight returns. The touchdowns are the obvious feature. The whole total matters because field position changes what the offense is asked to do. An efficient quarterback becomes more troublesome when the return game keeps offering him a shorter assignment. On Sunday, two of those assignments were reduced to watching.

The offense still did its own work. Gronkaludon caught five passes for 87 yards and a touchdown. Driflon Diggs caught seven for 73 and two scores. Ninjaskamara ran for 94 yards on ten attempts. There was no shortage of players prepared to fill the part of the scoreboard Flock had left for them.
I liked the first return. Then there was another kickoff. I tried to make that one useful, too.
body.speaker: Marshall Flock

body.text: That is an exceptionally mild description of a very rude afternoon for the Shadows. Docile is a nature; it isn't a promise to return the ball politely. I appreciate a player who can provide explosive plays without needing to narrate every yard afterward. The rest of us can handle the narrating. Some of us have considerable energy available for it.
A few matters for next week

Lavaridge comes to Mossdeep after losing 48–0 to Saffron. I expect the Eclipse to win. There, a prediction in ordinary language. I will not bury it under six conditional clauses until it becomes impossible to grade. If Mossdeep can't protect its quarterback and move the ball against this opponent, I'll have something less pleasant to write next week.

The checkable part is simple. Keep Marino upright, get productive early downs, and avoid turning the ball over to an opponent that badly needs help. I want to see the offense sustain drives even if the return game declines to score fourteen points. It is unreasonable to assign Flock two kickoff touchdowns every week. It is reasonable to ask the offense to remain good without them.

The defense has a particularly appealing chance to make Lavaridge's week longer. Saffron sacked Delphox four times. Mossdeep recorded four sacks against Fuchsia. That doesn't make the next total automatic, but it gives us a clear matchup to watch: can the Inferno keep their passer out of the long-yardage situations that fed Saffron's rush? If they can't, the Eclipse should have opportunities.

Electric Berry recovered a fumble and intercepted a pass against Fuchsia. Clay Rathews supplied two sacks. There are times when a defense's statistics become a long list of people enjoying the same afternoon. This was one of them. The useful question next week is whether the pressure and the tackling arrive before the game has become comfortable.

I don't need another 49–3 to believe Mossdeep belongs near the top of the league. I do need the ordinary parts to remain dependable: protection, possession, field position, finishing drives. A spectacular return can hide a stalled possession. A huge margin can make a loose quarter seem harmless. The pleasure of watching this team is that it has given us enough good football to discuss those details from first place.

Mt. Silver is unbeaten, too, and Saffron's defense is making an aggressive claim on everyone's attention. The competition is real. Mossdeep's case is real as well. Five wins, forty points allowed, and an offense with several ways to hurt a team is a very persuasive beginning.

So yes, I'll watch the protection next week. I'll watch the third downs and the injury report and all the things a responsible person should watch. I also reserve the right to enjoy a kickoff return that removes the need for any of those things for the next ninety-three yards. Flock has earned an audience. At five-and-zero, Mossdeep has earned one, too.

art.alt: Marshall Flock, Swellow No. 44, in Mossdeep magenta and gold on a kickoff return.

articles.title: Twelve carries? Cinnabar, pick up the ball
articles.dek: Dorian Pike has run out of patience with an offense that asked for another passing rescue and got a 23–16 loss in Dewford.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Twelve carries. Twenty-five rushing yards. There is your Cinnabar column, delivered early enough that someone might still use it. The Blaze went to Dewford, lost 23–16, and supplied the defense with another afternoon of waiting for the offense to decide whether it intended to possess the football for more than a philosophical moment.

I am furious because this team is good enough to make the fury worthwhile. Cinnabar is 3–2 with a plus-37 scoring margin. It can throw. It can defend. It can produce a game that looks perfectly manageable in the third quarter and still leave me staring at a fourth-down completion that wasn't remotely long enough. That last talent requires considerably less encouragement.

Exploud caught six passes for 97 yards and a touchdown. The quarterback threw for 223 yards. The Blaze led 16–10 after a third-quarter field goal. Nobody was being asked to climb out of an impossible hole. Cinnabar had a lead, time and an opportunity to make Dewford chase. It finished by chasing a touchdown itself.

The Breakers ran 36 times for 149 yards. Cinnabar ran twelve times for 25. Yes, those are different offenses. Yes, passing can be productive. I am aware of the modern world. I would also like my team to do something useful on the ground before its entire afternoon depends on another throw finding another receiver while the clock becomes everybody's least favorite participant.
The lead was there

Exploud's 28-yard touchdown catch gave Cinnabar a 13–10 lead with 5:11 left in the third. The next scoring drive produced a 36-yard field goal and a six-point advantage. At that stage, there was a perfectly serviceable route to a road win. Stop Dewford, possess the ball, add points if possible. The directions fit on a small card.

Dewford made a 44-yard field goal late in the quarter. The Blaze still led 16–13. Their next drive went fifty yards in ten plays and ended on downs with 4:55 remaining. Fifty yards of effort, no points, and a short interval before the defense was asked to return. This is the kind of drive that gets called promising by people who didn't need it to pay anything.

The Breakers answered with thirteen plays and 74 yards. Unfezant finished it with a ten-yard touchdown reception at 2:08. Cinnabar's six-point lead had become a four-point deficit. There is no mysterious explanation in the middle. Dewford assembled the drive it needed. The Blaze failed to stop it.

Then came the interception. Meowscarada returned it seventeen yards, and Dewford made a 37-yard field goal with 1:38 left. Now Cinnabar needed seven. A game the Blaze had led by six had become a one-drive emergency. I have seen enough emergencies in which the first suggestion is to ask the passer for a miracle. I would like a different departmental procedure.

The last possession began with a sack by Kricketune. Seven yards lost. Two incompletions followed, with Gumshoos and Mawile recording breakups. On fourth-and-seventeen, the completion to Wigglytuff gained seven. The arithmetic was accurate and absolutely useless. Dewford took over with 1:07 left and ended it.
The useful anger

I'm not going to demand forty runs because I am annoyed by twelve. A bad running play remains a bad running play if you perform it with conviction. The useful demand is that Cinnabar build a credible way to gain yards without asking the passing game to solve every difficult down. Twenty-five rushing yards doesn't make a defense spend much time worrying about the alternative.

A defense that can concentrate on the passer gets to make the obvious problem worse. The late sack wasn't merely seven yards. It changed the whole final possession, leaving Cinnabar trying to recover distance before it could pursue the first down. By the time the fourth-down throw arrived, seven yards had become an invitation to surrender the ball.

The Blaze also need to finish the drives they do extend. Ten plays and fifty yards should have been a chance to make Dewford's required answer more demanding. Instead, the Breakers needed one touchdown to lead. This is why I can't be satisfied by the passing yardage or Exploud's excellent day. Productive stretches have to purchase something.

I still like this offense's ability to create a long completion. Exploud demonstrated it. I still like a team that has scored 98 points while allowing 61. Those are reasons to demand better, not reasons to waive the complaint. Cinnabar has already shown enough capability that this loss feels avoidable rather than inevitable. That distinction is precisely what makes it so irritating.

Pewter comes next. The Rockers just won 12–10 on four field goals. They will happily accept a game in which every Cinnabar possession expires before it reaches the end zone. The Blaze should be able to ask more difficult questions than Rustboro did through the air. They also need to protect the ball well enough that Unown isn't handed another afternoon of manageable assignments.

I want an early lead and an offense that behaves as though it knows what to do with one. I want the fourth quarter to contain a productive possession before the final emergency. I want the running game to register as something more than the quiet space between passing attempts. These are not extravagant requests for a club that considers itself a contender.

Cinnabar can beat Pewter. I expect it to. If the Blaze give me another useful-looking loss and twelve ornamental carries, the next column will be less polite. I recognize that some readers may find that threat difficult to distinguish from the current column. Watch the rushing total. I'll make the difference clear.

art.alt: Cinnabar orange and gold helmet beside a football on stadium turf.

articles.title: The trade was completed. The explanation is still due.
articles.dek: Ellis Quill on Milotic’s extraordinary return, Sunyshore’s first defeat, and the danger of letting one afternoon write the whole transaction history.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Milotic made the trade story wonderfully easy to tell and rather harder to evaluate. Sunyshore sent him to Violet in Week 5. Against his former team, he returned an interception for a touchdown, forced and recovered a fumble, and finished as the defensive player of the game. Violet won 33–20. If you were designing a memorable first chapter, restraint would probably have prevented you from using all of that.

The first chapter is real. The final judgment isn't available yet. I expect that distinction to survive approximately three seconds of discussion, because nobody who watched Milotic run fifty-two yards with Jolt Vick's pass wants to begin by discussing the rest of the package. I don't particularly want to begin there either. The cornerback earned the opening paragraph.

What interests me is the pressure this puts on Sunyshore's explanation. The Starseekers were unbeaten. They traded six players for four. One of the departures then supplied the clearest difference in their first loss. A manager can have a defensible plan and still endure a dreadful afternoon. This was a very public test of that possibility.

The actual outgoing group was Audino, Milotic, Frillish, Minccino, Poltchageist and Numel. Violet sent Buizel, Eelektrik, Anorith and Slakoth. There were no picks. Those names matter because a six-for-four exchange can't honestly be reduced to one cornerback forever, even when that cornerback makes the first game feel like a personal editorial intervention.
The plays make the case

Milotic's interception came late in the first quarter. Violet already led 6–0. He took Vick's deep-left throw fifty-two yards the other way, and the extra point made it 13–0. That changed the immediate task for an offense already working without DeZhaun Watzon. Sunyshore now needed to recover two scores rather than settle into a competitive game.

The forced fumble mattered in a different way. Nair Jordan caught a short-right pass late in the second quarter and lost the ball. Milotic recovered. Violet's next snap was Iron Jugulis's four-yard touchdown pass to Carnivine. The cornerback didn't score that touchdown himself, but he supplied the possession and the position. Giving him credit requires no imaginative accounting.

He also broke up a third-quarter pass intended for Fera Gatr. The interception and fumble are louder. The breakup belongs in the same account because it shows his afternoon wasn't confined to two unusual moments. He made another ordinary defensive play in a game where Sunyshore would have appreciated one more successful throw.
I didn't take the whole trade onto the field. Just my number. It seemed to be enough luggage.
body.speaker: Milotic

body.text: I like that answer more than any promise of permanent vindication. A player can enjoy this game without predicting the next ten. So can the rest of us. Milotic's performance was exceptional, and Sunyshore will have to live with it. Neither statement needs a claim about what every other player in the exchange will eventually become.
Violet still had to finish

There is another danger in a perfect trade narrative: it can make the winning team's later work disappear. Violet led 26–20 late in the third quarter. The early defensive touchdowns and field position hadn't ended the game. The Falcons still needed to protect a six-point lead against a team that had already scored twenty.

They answered with a 75-yard touchdown drive. A sack made the possession harder. Zangoose converted third-and-ten with an eleven-yard run. Furret caught a 26-yard deep-right pass. Jugulis finished the series with a one-yard run for a touchdown at 4:38. Those plays are part of the victory, too. Milotic gave Violet a remarkable advantage; the offense eventually supplied the drive that made it hold.

Furret finished with seven catches for 147 yards. The completions included gains of 44, 28, 26 and 24. That is a substantial receiving performance to have sharing a headline with a cornerback's reunion. Violet didn't merely wait for the former Starseeker to do everything. It generated its own explosive plays and found a crucial late conversion on the ground.

Sunyshore outgained Violet 286–272, earned more first downs and converted six of twelve third downs to the Falcons' two of seven. Those numbers don't reverse the score. They do help explain why the game remained close enough to require that last long drive. The Starseekers could move the ball. The turnovers made their successful possessions more expensive to replace.
What comes after the headline

At 4–1, Sunyshore still has a very good record. Watzon is clear of the injury report. Veilstone visits next, giving the Starseekers an immediate chance to show how the new roster works with their starting quarterback available again. That is a more useful next test than asking them to defend the trade in the abstract after every practice.

I will watch whether they protect possession and whether their offense finishes drives. I will also watch the roles of the incoming players over time. A transaction's eventual value depends on what a team receives and uses, as well as what it gives away. One spectacular revenge game can't supply all of those answers. It can make the questions much less comfortable.

Violet goes to Mahogany at 2–3, with an opportunity to turn its biggest win into a more sustained recovery. That matters for the Falcons, who are entitled to a story about their own future rather than permanent employment as the supporting cast in Sunyshore's embarrassment. They have Milotic now. They also have a receiver who just gained 147 yards and an offense that finished the decisive drive.

For this week, however, the headline belongs where it belongs. Sunyshore traded Milotic. Milotic helped beat Sunyshore. The longer transaction analysis can wait for more football. The film from this afternoon already has its author.

articles.title: Miltank leads the backs; Stakataka needs a job
articles.dek: Calvin Rook ranks twelve from the 31 visible HB/FB prospects and puts one Rustboro development bet on the record.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Last week belonged to quarterbacks. This week the board turns to halfbacks and fullbacks, which should not be treated as interchangeable ways to own a large overall number. Miltank leads my running-back discussion; Stakataka has a formidable visible band and a job question attached. An offense needs to know how it will use a fullback before admiring one into an expensive selection.

The thirty-one visible prospects supply age, level, scouting ranges, universities and combine results. They do not supply a college rushing season for me to invent. My comparisons are about possible assignments. Philly just ran for ninety-seven yards in a loss; Lynch’s injury makes Mt. Silver’s backfield depth immediate news. A back can have a valuable job without being a cure for every problem around it.

At eleven, I have Rustboro’s Tympole ahead of a stronger current band. That is an admitted development bet on the movement testing, with a university I happen to enjoy discussing. Keep the receipt. The board is an opinion about the visible evidence, not a claim to hidden grades or a guarantee about future evolution.

prospects.name: Miltank
prospects.analysis: The best blend of starting grade and movement on this board. Miltank’s 4.72 forty leads this selected group, with a forty-inch vertical and twenty-two bench reps. I see a back worth building a real rushing assignment around, while keeping the broad grade band in view.
prospects.concern: A workout cannot establish ball security or vision.

prospects.name: Zangoose
prospects.analysis: Zangoose is close enough to make the first place an argument. A 4.75 forty, forty-inch vertical and 6.60 cone make the movement case. I give Miltank the edge on the current visible band, but an offense seeking a different rushing profile should keep both names open.

prospects.name: Stakataka
prospects.analysis: Stakataka has the strongest visible band of these backs and twenty-seven bench reps. Fullback is a different assignment from leading a rushing attack. Draft a defined job: blocking, short yardage and useful snaps alongside another back, rather than purchasing an impressive number without a role.
prospects.concern: A 5.23 forty and 7.28 cone limit the movement argument.
prospects.projection: Premium FB if the job exists

prospects.name: Druddigon
prospects.analysis: Druddigon offers another strong starting point at fullback. Twenty-three bench reps support a physical assignment, and the visible band reaches ninety-nine. I would ask the offense exactly how often it expects to use that assignment before spending an early selection.
prospects.concern: The 5.11 forty is part of the cost.

prospects.name: Deerling
prospects.analysis: Deerling’s 6.53 cone is the most interesting number here. I want to explore the movement without pretending it supplies rushing production by itself. The lower visible band asks for patience, but there is enough in the testing to keep the conversation near the top of the HB list.
prospects.concern: Eleven bench reps offer less strength evidence than the leaders.

prospects.name: Nidorino
prospects.analysis: Nidorino has a useful middle starting band and a 4.90 forty. The case is less dramatic than the first two halfbacks and more substantial than a pure late speculation. I would prefer a clear rotation plan over immediate promises of a lead role.
prospects.concern: No single workout number settles the role.

prospects.name: Parasect
prospects.analysis: Parasect brings twenty bench reps and a relatively strong visible band to a fullback conversation that should remain about assignments. A team that actually fields the position can make a sensible case. A team that rarely does should keep its enthusiasm on paper.
prospects.concern: The 7.11 cone requires realistic movement expectations.

prospects.name: Ariados
prospects.analysis: Ariados offers seventeen bench reps and a thirty-two-inch vertical. The starting band keeps it in the useful fullback group. I would compare the expected blocking and short-yardage workload directly with Parasect before deciding which profile deserves the earlier investment.
prospects.concern: A 5.06 forty will not make the speed argument.

prospects.name: Kecleon
prospects.analysis: Kecleon’s 6.96 cone gives this fullback profile a little more movement interest. The band is broad enough that I would avoid a confident declaration about immediate quality. Give the prospect a specific job and compare the cost with the existing roster.
prospects.concern: Fourteen bench reps trail several fullbacks above.

prospects.name: Kecleon
prospects.analysis: The second Kecleon is a separate player from a separate university. Similar species and bands do not make them interchangeable. This one has a 5.09 forty and 7.05 cone; those results place it slightly below the Pyrite prospect on my current list.
prospects.concern: Keep identity and workout differences straight.

prospects.name: Tympole
prospects.analysis: Here is my reach. Rustboro’s Tympole has a 4.86 forty, thirty-nine-inch vertical and 6.62 cone. The visible band is only 28–56. I am placing the movement ahead of a stronger current band below, and the Rustboro connection makes this an especially easy bet for me to like.
prospects.concern: Seven bench reps and the low band demand patience.

prospects.name: Minccino
prospects.analysis: Minccino has a stronger current band than Tympole and a forty-inch vertical. A more cautious board could reverse those two. Mine currently values the Rustboro prospect’s movement a little more. Neither should be advertised as an immediate answer simply because the price might be low.
prospects.concern: A 4.95 forty tempers the explosive-workout claim.

articles.title: The confidence meter: Mossdeep takes the top spot
articles.dek: Saffron climbs, Mt. Silver loses Lynch, and Sunyshore receives a very pointed trade review. Rowan Vale ranks all 32.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Mossdeep goes first. Saffron goes second. Mt. Silver remains unbeaten and moves down two places because the rankings are a judgment about the next game, too. Losing Lynch for six weeks changes that judgment. I expect objections. Please include a proposed way to replace 672 rushing yards when submitting one.

This week's theme is confidence: who makes me comfortable when the next game begins? Dewford has earned more trust by making Mossdeep work and beating Cinnabar. Violet has made Sunyshore less comfortable in a particularly memorable way. Every club gets a setting, and every movement compares with the published Week 4 list.

rankings.text: The return game supplied two touchdowns and the offense supplied five more in a 49–3 win. Moving the Eclipse above Mt. Silver feels overdue after a week in which their protection survived the missing tackle and the Reds lost Lynch. Plus-163 is a persuasive opening argument.

Forty-eight points on the road and a third shutout. Lamb gained 266 yards from scrimmage; Brooks recorded four sacks. I trust this defense against anyone, and the offense keeps offering additional reasons to make that trust unpleasant for the next opponent.

The Reds won 24–20 because they found a late field goal and made the final defensive plays. They remain unbeaten. Losing Lynch for six weeks makes the next version of their running game a real question, even after Vibrava helped finish the winning possession.

The narrow loss to Mossdeep looked encouraging. Beating Cinnabar 23–16 makes it more encouraging. Dewford ran for 149 yards and put together the touchdown drive it needed in the fourth quarter. I trust the Breakers to make a favored opponent work.

Milotic made his former club regret its forwarding arrangements. The Starseekers still moved the ball and return Watzon to a team with a 4–1 record. I expect a recovery. I would prefer that the next defensive star not arrive wearing an opponent’s jersey.

The passing game can hurt a defense, but twelve carries for 25 yards gives an opponent a fairly small list of concerns. Cinnabar led in Dewford and failed to finish. Pewter is a useful opportunity to demonstrate that the fourth quarter can be handled more sensibly.

A 13–10 win over Celadon adds another victory without ending every question about the distance between Petalburg and the best teams. At 4–1, the record deserves respect. The next visit to Mauville should tell us whether the offense can produce a less anxious finish.

The bye preserved a 3–1 record and a plus-three margin. Vermilion has the opening win over Saffron on its receipt; I have read it. Cerulean now supplies a fresh opportunity to make the offense’s case without pointing exclusively at September’s best sentence.

Lavender needed this one after Mt. Silver. Two late recoveries protected a 17–15 win at Hearthome, and a 52-yard field goal made the two-point try necessary. Four wins buy a pleasant bye. Two-of-eleven on third down supplies something to discuss during it.

Milotic deserves the cover, but Furret’s 147 receiving yards and the long fourth-quarter touchdown drive deserve pages inside. Violet has a 2–3 record and a win over Sunyshore. Follow it with something useful at Mahogany, and the discussion changes again.

Another two-point win, this time 14–12 over Pastoria, leaves Blackthorn 4–1 with a plus-one margin. Those victories count. They also make me reluctant to describe the record as evidence of a large advantage over the teams immediately below. Enjoy the bye; keep the receipt.

Veilstone beat Mahogany 14–9 and moved to 3–2. The season margin is only plus-one, so the next trip to Sunyshore is a considerably more demanding demonstration. Keep it close, protect possession, and give the Starseekers another uncomfortable afternoon before claiming a larger rise.

A 22–20 road win at Mauville puts Viridian above .500. The next trip is to winless Celadon, which makes this a chance to consolidate rather than merely celebrate. A narrow win is useful. Requiring one every week makes the confidence meter work overtime.

The 16–13 overtime loss to Azalea is an unwelcome result for a team with a plus-nineteen season margin. Snowpoint has shown enough to remain here, but the evidence now needs victories. Eterna arrives with its own interest in an orderly, low-scoring game.

A 21–18 overtime win over Cianwood moves Canalave to 3–2 despite a negative scoring margin. The Bulwark keep giving themselves a chance. Oreburgh just made Mt. Silver work to the end, so the next opponent is unlikely to regard a close contest as a crisis.

The 2–2 record and plus-three margin survived the bye. A visit to Snowpoint gives Eterna an immediate chance to make its position more interesting. I want to see an offense that can finish a drive rather than rely on the opponent making the final mistake.

Overtime took a 21–18 result away in Canalave. Cianwood remains competitive and has a positive margin, but Mt. Silver now visits. Testing the Reds’ running game without Lynch is the obvious invitation. Letting Alakazam have an easy afternoon would be a poor response.

Twenty-four points should buy a useful chance to win. Allowing thirty at Sootopolis made that chance disappear. Cerulean can throw, but the defense has allowed 93 points through five games. Vermilion is the next opportunity to keep the opponent within the offense’s reach.

Unown made all four field goals in Rustboro, including two from 52. That is excellent kicking and a very narrow description of a complete offense. Cinnabar will probably ask for more points than the Rockers needed this week. A touchdown would be an agreeable beginning.

Philly ran for 97 yards and a touchdown in a 12–10 loss. Two fumbles and the missed late field goal made the rushing advantage insufficient. Dewford is a difficult place to seek forgiveness. Frosmoth’s ten completions in twenty-six attempts need an immediate improvement.

Olivine returns from its bye at 2–2 with a negative margin. Azalea brings a first victory and considerably less interest in being treated as a convenient opponent. This is a chance to make a middle-table record look like the beginning of something useful.

The margin for the season is only minus-one. The record is 1–4. That combination will encourage some readers and exhaust others. Violet arrives with the Milotic story still ringing, and Mahogany needs to turn another competitive game into a different final result.

The Miners nearly turned Plusico’s late fumble into an upset of Mt. Silver. They still lost 24–20. That effort merits more respect than a casual reading of 1–4, but close losses are becoming an expensive collection. Canalave offers the next chance to stop collecting.

A 30–24 win over Cerulean is a welcome use of an offense that has not consistently outrun the damage at the other end. Sootopolis has allowed 130 points. Fortree visits next, and a cleaner defensive game would make the progress easier to trust.

Pastoria lost 14–12 to Blackthorn and sits 2–3. The defense kept the game available; the final points remained elsewhere. Hearthome comes next with a similarly painful two-point loss. Both teams will be perfectly capable of explaining why they need this one.

A 22–20 loss to Viridian dropped Mauville below .500. The Dynamos have allowed 101 points, which makes a narrow offensive miss unusually costly. Petalburg brings a 4–1 record. Mauville needs possessions that end with its own points and fewer reasons for the defense to return.

The first win arrived 16–13 in overtime at Snowpoint. It does not erase four defeats or a minus-52 margin. It does give Azalea something tangible to take to Olivine, where another competitive game would make the first victory feel less isolated.

The missed extra point, failed two-point try and late fumble all fit inside a 17–15 loss to Lavender. Hearthome had time to win and lost the ball instead. At Pastoria, possession and finishing chances should matter more than any new inspirational language.

Saffron won 48–0. Mossdeep is next. There are kinder sequences on the schedule, but the Inferno need a practical response: protect Delphox, find manageable downs and get points before the margin becomes a separate opponent. Three-of-sixteen on third down cannot travel comfortably.

The 13–10 loss at Petalburg was competitive. Celadon is still 0–5. A visit from Viridian supplies another plausible chance, but thirty-seven points in five games leaves very little room for an ordinary defensive mistake. The offense must make a close game less fragile.

A bye paused an 0–4 start. It did not repair the minus-41 margin. Sootopolis has just allowed 24 points in a win, so Fortree should see an opportunity to move the ball. The other half of that invitation is stopping an opponent that just scored thirty.

Mossdeep scored 49 and allowed three. Fuchsia now gets Saffron, which just scored 48 and allowed none. The immediate ambition is concrete: protect the ball and make the opponent sustain ordinary drives. Giving away another return touchdown would make a hard assignment even harder.

articles.title: Week 6: fifteen games, fifteen ways to check the picks
articles.dek: Mt. Silver begins life without Lynch; Watzon returns; Mossdeep and Saffron face teams coming off heavy defeats.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: I went seven-and-seven on the first saved panel slate. Rowan led at ten-and-four; Dorian went eight-and-six, Mara six-and-eight, Ellis five-and-nine. The score guesses have a separate closest-score bonus, shared when writers tie. Those bonuses do not change the win-loss record. This is our first graded slate, so nobody gets to borrow an imaginary season of prior success.

The Week 6 keys below are things we can inspect afterward. They are useful targets, not promises that meeting one automatically wins a game. Lavender and Blackthorn have byes. The other thirty teams have work, and the five panelists have fifteen more opportunities to explain themselves.

matchups.analysis: Viridian escaped Mauville by two; Celadon lost at Petalburg by three. I favor the visitors, but the winless record should not persuade Viridian to offer free possessions. A patient rushing game gives the Titans a way to keep Celadon from making one late scoring drive decisive.
matchups.awayKey: Finish at least two touchdown drives and avoid a lost fumble.
matchups.homeKey: Keep Viridian below twenty and make the fourth quarter a one-score contest.

matchups.matchup: Cinnabar’s pass protection against Pewter’s disruption
matchups.analysis: The Blaze should have enough passing offense to beat a team that needed four field goals in Rustboro. The warning is the late sack and interception in Dewford. Pewter will welcome short fields; Cinnabar must make the Rockers drive for their chances.
matchups.awayKey: Turn one takeaway into points and reach the end zone.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no more than one sack and improve on the twenty-five rushing yards in Dewford.

matchups.matchup: Cerulean’s passing game against a rested defense
matchups.analysis: Cerulean scored twenty-four and still lost to Sootopolis. Vermilion returns from a bye at 3–1 with a slim scoring margin. I lean toward the rested home team in a close game, but the Dragons can change that judgment if their passing production comes with fewer defensive concessions.
matchups.awayKey: Keep Vermilion below twenty points and avoid giving away a short field.
matchups.homeKey: Make Cerulean sustain drives and score a touchdown before halftime.

matchups.analysis: Saffron has allowed twenty points in five games. Fuchsia has just lost 49–3. The Psi Corps are a heavy favorite for good reason. Brooks’s four-sack afternoon in Lavaridge supplies the most obvious matchup; Fuchsia needs a way to keep an early deficit from turning every possession into a passing-down emergency.
matchups.awayKey: Force at least three sacks and protect possession.
matchups.homeKey: Avoid a return touchdown and convert at least four third downs.

matchups.matchup: Azalea’s confidence against a rested opponent
matchups.analysis: Azalea finally won, taking an overtime result in Snowpoint. Olivine has had a bye to prepare and still owns the better record. I give the home team a slight edge, while asking whether Azalea can follow its first victory with another game that remains available in the fourth quarter.
matchups.awayKey: Reach halftime within one score and avoid two turnovers.
matchups.homeKey: Score touchdowns on two trips inside the twenty rather than relying entirely on kicks.

matchups.analysis: Mt. Silver must begin six weeks without Lynch. Vibrava helped close the Oreburgh game, but a larger weekly assignment will be a fresh test. Cianwood just lost in overtime at Canalave. I favor the Reds’ passing offense, with their early-down rushing efficiency the most useful thing to inspect.
matchups.awayKey: Average four yards per rush and avoid a lost fumble.
matchups.homeKey: Hold the Reds below twenty-five points and force Alakazam into third-and-long.

matchups.matchup: Furret’s explosive catches against Mahogany’s coverage
matchups.analysis: Violet comes off its best result; Mahogany comes off another narrow loss. Furret’s four catches of at least twenty-four yards at Sunyshore make the perimeter matchup particularly interesting. I narrowly favor Violet, but asking the Falcons to repeat the turnover production would be a poor foundation for the pick.
matchups.awayKey: Create two completions of twenty yards and win without needing a defensive touchdown.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no completion of thirty yards and finish two touchdown drives.

matchups.analysis: Rustboro ran well and lost to Pewter because its passing game and ball security failed at the wrong times. Dewford has just beaten Cinnabar and looks the more dependable team. The Stone need a productive Philly game that also leaves room for Frosmoth to complete throws when the Breakers expect them.
matchups.awayKey: Lose no fumbles and complete at least half the passing attempts.
matchups.homeKey: Keep Philly below a hundred yards and finish two touchdown drives.

matchups.analysis: Petalburg’s 4–1 record includes a narrow escape against Celadon. Mauville lost by two to Viridian and has allowed 101 points. I lean toward the Pride, while wanting a more assertive offensive afternoon than the one that produced thirteen points last week.
matchups.awayKey: Score twenty points and avoid a negative turnover margin.
matchups.homeKey: Keep Petalburg under twenty and turn one takeaway into a scoring drive.

matchups.analysis: The Eclipse are 5–0 and Armstead is clear of the injury report. Lavaridge arrives after a shutout and four sacks allowed. Mossdeep should win comfortably if Marino has time and the offense sustains drives without requiring another pair of Flock return touchdowns.
matchups.awayKey: Allow fewer than three sacks and score before halftime.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Lavaridge below four third-down conversions and protect Marino to one sack or fewer.

matchups.matchup: Fortree’s defense against an encouraged offense
matchups.analysis: Sootopolis just scored thirty against Cerulean. Fortree returns from a bye still seeking its first win. Neither defense has earned comfortable trust. I prefer the home team’s recent offensive evidence, with the caveat that Sootopolis’s 130 points allowed leaves visitors plenty of reason to keep playing.
matchups.awayKey: Score on the opening two possessions or force two takeaways.
matchups.homeKey: Keep Fortree below twenty and produce two touchdown drives.

matchups.matchup: Oreburgh’s finishing against Canalave’s close-game defense
matchups.analysis: The Miners pushed Mt. Silver to the final possession. Canalave survived overtime against Cianwood. This should be competitive, and I lean toward the home side’s ability to find the final points. Oreburgh has to turn respectable resistance into a victory before its record becomes impossible to explain away.
matchups.awayKey: Convert half the third downs and score a touchdown in the fourth quarter.
matchups.homeKey: Win the turnover margin and keep Oreburgh below twenty-four.

matchups.analysis: Snowpoint lost an overtime game it will feel it could have won. Eterna returns from a bye at 2–2. I slightly prefer the home team, but the deciding evidence should be ordinary: which offense can turn a long possession into seven rather than leave the kicker to settle everything?
matchups.awayKey: Score two touchdowns and avoid a lost fumble.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Eterna below twenty and finish the final scoring opportunity.

matchups.matchup: Two frustrated offenses against the clock
matchups.analysis: Hearthome and Pastoria both lost by two. The Haunts fumbled their last chance against Lavender; Pastoria finished two points short of Blackthorn. I favor the home side by a field goal, with possession security more convincing than any claim that either club is due a comfortable afternoon.
matchups.awayKey: Lose no fumbles and make every extra point.
matchups.homeKey: Score two touchdowns and avoid surrendering a late short field.

matchups.analysis: Sunyshore gets its starting quarterback back after the Milotic reunion loss. Veilstone arrives at 3–2 after beating Mahogany. I expect the Starseekers to recover, but the defense must make Veilstone earn its points while the offense avoids repeating the giveaways that made Violet’s afternoon possible.
matchups.awayKey: Keep Sunyshore below twenty-four and produce two takeaways.
matchups.homeKey: Lose no fumbles and convert at least half the third downs.
